title: The Bank That Failed the Freed, and Who Controls Black Money Now | The Long View, Ep. 1
lede: Control of Congress changed hands this week. In 1865, Congress chartered the Freedman's Savings and Trust Company for four million newly freed people; when oversight failed, depositors got back 62 cents on the dollar. This first episode of The Long View follows that question from 1865 to now: who controls the money, and does it reach Black depositors? Plus the week's African markets, Friday's jobs report, new Black governors, the Caribbean's freight fight and the dates to watch.
keyPoints: Black unemployment fell to 6.6% in October from 7.0% in September; the overall rate was 4.1% and payrolls rose 165,000 (BLS, Nov 6).
AP called the Senate and CBS News and AP the House for Democrats; Mississippi's Senate race remained uncalled, with certification due Nov 13.
The Freedman's Bank took in more than $57 million from about 70,000 depositors before it closed in 1874; repayment came to 62% of what was owed (National Archives).
Black-owned banks fell from 48 in 2001 to 21 in 2019 (FDIC); on Nov 4, Mechanics and Farmers Bank shareholders approved its sale to Optus, pending regulators (American Banker).
Caribbean businesses asked the U.S. to make the region's exemptions from maritime fees permanent; the current pause ends Nov 9 (Jamaica Observer, gCaptain).
